body:
I always assumed this was intentional, and was surprised of people expecting the opposite.

In fact, at some point, I relied on the fact that the preloaded instances remain there to have resource based communication: If I preload the same resource in two scripts, I know they will always share an instance, so this resource can be a channel for otherwise disconnected parts of the code to talk. *I do not rely on this anymore, I have build a bespoke solution.*

My recommendation for scenes - in particular stages - is background loading with a progress bar, so the game is not unresponsive, and you do not run into cyclic dependencies. You'll find that what is easy to do, is not necessarily the best for a large game, and Godot has done a lot to remove the getting started friction, but not so much for the big games. And this is another example.

> I always assumed this was intentional, and was surprised of people expecting the opposite.
> 
> In fact, at some point, I relied on the fact that the preloaded instances remain there to have resource based communication: If I preload the same resource in two scripts, I know they will always share an instance, so this resource can be a channel for otherwise disconnected parts of the code to talk. *I do not rely on this anymore, I have build a bespoke solution.*

It is indeed pretty clear that resource caching and sharing is intentional, if a resource path is loaded when a resource currently in memory is associated with that path (including the use of `Resource.take_over_path()`, because cached paths don't need to correspond to an actual file). However, ResourceLoader keeps these cached entries using weak references (object IDs), so the cache does not contribute to the reference count of resources, meaning they are only held in memory as long as you have at least one script variable or object property referencing that resource directly (not an object ID or WeakRef).

The issue at hand is specifically about GDScript-preloaded resources never being freed, even if you release all user-created RefCounted objects and free all non-RefCounted ones that reference scripts with these preloads (scripts themselves seem to be sticky and never unloaded, and hold preloads directly). Other forms of dependency loading (`@export` and ResourcePreloader) do respect reference counting, and allow depended resources to be freed if you do not keep any references to the scene or resource using them, as seen in the MRP.

Even if this behavior is changed (not only documented and warned about), projects could still explicitly hold "eternal" references to resources in some autoload or static var (without `@static_unload`, just in case that gets fixed as well).

Edit: I see what you mean about resources sticking around even if you don't keep any references to them. Yes, that would definitely be a breaking change that should be mentioned in the release notes and migration guide, if approved. But also, if there's a reference cycle between the resources, then they just stay forever regardless since that's another thing with reference counting.

Here's a slightly different MRP:

[preload_test.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26763452/preload_test.zip)

The problem is not that preloaded resources are not unloaded, but it's the script itself that's never getting unloaded. If the script was freed properly, the same would happen to its resources.

Sounds like some weird GDScript cache bug.
